transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-17
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, Lighthouse AI), Alex Rivera (Head of ML), Omar Patel (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen; imperfect):
Lighthouse is evaluating Redwood for a mixed workload with steady inference traffic plus unpredictable marketing-driven spikes. Main asks: reserved GPU sizing, tenant isolation (multi-tenant model serving), warm pool / prewarm strategy for sub-100ms p95 on small prompts, and data residency/KMS concerns. They want a pilot to validate burst economics and failover behavior.

Topics: sizing, isolation topology, burst model, warm pools, SLA tradeoffs, pilot scope, SOC2/KMS, pricing model

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro — I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood Dedicated team, and Priya's our solutions engineer.
[00:18] Maya (CTO): Hi all. We are Maya, Alex and Omar. Quick context: Lighthouse runs a mixture of chat assistants and realtime enrichment pipelines, so steady qps plus periodic marketing spikes. We're trying to understand if reserved GPUs make sense versus hosted bursting.
[00:35] Priya (SE): Great, thanks. Can you share ballpark numbers? steady qps, peak qps, latency SLOs, and any isolation constraints?
[00:48] Alex (Head of ML): Baseline is about 250 qps across endpoints, peaks up to 3k qps for 15-30 minutes on promo pushes. P95 target is 120ms for short prompts, we can tolerate up to 300ms for long multimodal jobs.
[01:12] Omar (SRE): Also, we need tenant isolation because some of our customers require contractual isolation and per-tenant throughput caps. VPC requirements are likely.
[01:24] Jordan: Good, that helps. So two threads — capacity sizing for the steady+burst profile and isolation/topology. For sizing, we'd model a Dedicated pool with warm nodes plus burst to hosted or spare nodes. For isolation there are a couple of approaches: full single-tenant nodes, tenant fencing via scheduling, or soft isolation (resource guarantees).
[01:45] Priya: To add — our warm-pool pattern is typically a prewarmed set of reserved nodes pinned to a model family. During bursts, we use fast fallback to a compatible quantized variant in Redwood Hosted with routing rules. That reduces cold-start risk and cost.
[02:05] Alex: When you say "compatible quantized variant" — is that on the same model weights? How do you ensure parity of outputs for quality checks?
[02:14] Priya: It's a tradeoff. The quantized variant will be close but not bit-for-bit identical; we recommend running the candidate prompts through evals we provide. You can also pin critical endpoints to always run on Dedicated unquantized nodes.
[02:32] Maya: About isolation — our legal team wants per-tenant audit logs, separate KMS keys for a small set of customers, and the ability to prove no noisy-neighbor effect. Can Redwood do per-tenant KMS and audit ingestion?
[02:45] Jordan: Yes — in Redwood Private or Dedicated with VPC, we support customer KMS integrations and audit logs. For Dedicated we can enable tenant-level RBAC and separate key scopes. Note: some of those features are part of Enterprise packages, we'll include those in the pricing sheet.
[03:08] Omar: In terms of topology, we're worried about blast radius during preemption or failover. If a preemption happens, what's the expected recovery pattern? We need failover to degrade gracefully not blow the whole cluster.
[03:20] Priya: We have two mechanisms — model-level fallback and regional fallback. If a reserved pool is preempted, traffic can be re-routed by policy to a warm pool or hosted nodes. There's a short latency spike during reroute. We can configure canary percentages to shift traffic gradually.
[03:40] Alex: How fast is prewarm? The marketing spikes are 10-30 minutes; we need most capacity warmed within 3-4 minutes ideally.
[03:50] Priya: Warm pools are kept with running processes, so new worker availability is immediate for the pinned model. Starting fresh GPU instances takes longer; that's why warm pools are recommended for short spikes. The prewarm cutover is on the order of seconds to <1 minute for warm workers.
[04:08] Jordan: Cost tradeoffs — warm pools cost more than cold scaling but lower p95 latency. We'll provide a burst-cost model that shows token and node-level economics.
[04:20] Maya: We also care about versioning and rollouts. If we roll a new model, can we do a canary to 5% of traffic and auto-fallback?
[04:28] Priya: Yes — Redwood Console supports canaries and automatic fallback to previous model variants if latency or quality regressions are detected.
[04:36] Omar: A few technical clarifications: do you support KV cache sharing across instances, and how's stateful cache maintained during scaling?
[04:46] Priya: We support prefix and KV caching with sticky routing; when a request hits a different worker the KV cache miss may increase but we have a distributed cache layer. Slight note — auto transcription sometimes writes that as "K V c ash" — but it's KV cache.
[04:59] Alex: (laughs) Noted. On fallback routing — can we route only certain endpoints to hosted fallback while keeping sensitive customers on Dedicated?
[05:06] Jordan: Absolutely. You can route by route/model or by customer tag. So critical tenants can stay on Dedicated and others burst to hosted.
[05:15] Maya: Compliance — SOC2 is a must, and we need encryption at rest with customer-managed keys. Any on-prem option?
[05:22] Priya: Yes to both. On-prem is available via Redwood Private; Dedicated in a VPC can also use customer KMS. SOC2 docs we'll share (redacted) after this call.
[05:34] Omar: Network egress — our billing dept worries about cross-region egress if the fallback hits hosted in a different cloud region. Can routing be constrained to region?
[05:43] Priya: Yes, routing policies include region constraints and cost tiers. We'll set preferred regions and fallback regions to avoid egress surprises.
[05:52] Alex: Let's talk SLAs and SLOs — what's the committed p95 under Dedicated?
[05:58] Jordan: Dedicated SLAs are uptime-first; latency SLOs depend on instance sizing and prewarm strategy. We'll recommend hardware profiles for your p95 target and include them in the sizing doc.
[06:10] Maya: What about multi-GPU models and sequence-length variation — our jobs vary from short prompts to 2k token sequences for context retrieval. How does batch sizing interact?
[06:21] Priya: Our runtime does continuous batching and dynamic kernel selection. For long sequences we recommend separate routes or different worker pools to avoid polluting latency for short prompts. That's a sizing knob.
[06:34] Omar: Any rough guidance for reserved GPU count? With 250qps steady and 3k burst, what would be starting point?
[06:42] Priya: Rough back-of-envelope: if an n1/gpu can handle ~100 qps for your model (depends on batch), you'd need ~3 nodes for steady 250 qps with headroom, and warm-pool + burst to cover the additional 2.75k qps — which could be served by hosted fallbacks or extra reserved nodes depending on cost appetite. We'll run a more accurate simulation in the spreadsheet.
[07:05] Alex: We want to keep costs predictable. Could the pilot be a 2-week test with a capped monthly commit then evaluate?
[07:12] Jordan: Yes, we often do time-limited pilots with a small reserved commit to validate latency and cost. Post-pilot you can scale reservation.
[07:20] Maya: For the pilot, we need to measure noisy neighbor observability and eviction behavior. Can we get traces and token-level cost breakdowns?
[07:29] Priya: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency, and traces. We can enable increased observability during pilot.
[07:36] Omar: Are there known gotchas about using our internal model registry? We use MLFlow and CI/CD to push models.
[07:44] Priya: We have integrations and a model onboarding process. CI can push to Redwood model catalog via APIs. We'll document that flow. There can be slight naming mismatch sometimes in autometa, we surface a mapping table.
[07:58] Alex: Any examples of similar customers? We want references for regulated verticals.
[08:03] Jordan: We have a few healthcare and fintech customers on Dedicated with KMS and private VPC deployments; we'll include anonymized case blurbs in the follow-up.
[08:13] Maya: Ok, a weird question — if we want per-tenant KMS keys for five customers only, is that friction?
[08:21] Jordan: Not friction — it's supported. We'll map keys to tenant scopes and include that in the architecture diagram.
[08:29] Omar: On preemption, how do you handle partial warm pool exhaustion during an extended spike? I.e., if warm nodes are exhausted and hosted fallback is saturated too, what's the graceful degradation?
[08:40] Priya: We recommend shaping policies and backpressure — route less-critical endpoints to lower-cost quantized variants and degrade non-critical features. Also set per-route rate limits and token caps.
[08:52] Alex: We might consider hybrid: some reserved nodes for the highest value endpoints and hosted for the rest.
[08:58] Jordan: That's common. We can also create a hotpool for the top 10% endpoints and a warmpool for the next 30%.
[09:07] Maya: Can Redwood run canary experiments on the quantized variants to measure quality delta?
[09:12] Priya: Yes — Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and run A/B quality checks versus baseline prompts.
[09:20] Omar: Security question: for Dedicated nodes in our VPC — do you expose SSH or how do you troubleshoot?
[09:27] Jordan: We don't expose SSH to customer VMs; debugging is via logs, traces, and we can provide secure bastion-assisted debugging sessions for on-prem. For Private on-prem installs, different support model applies.
[09:40] Alex: About contract/commit size — if we commit to 50% steady capacity for 6 months, can we adjust midscope if usage grows?
[09:49] Jordan: Contracts have change control; we support headroom adjustments and pools resizing. We'll include typical change clauses in the commercial proposal.
[09:58] Maya: Let's nail the pilot scope now — what should be included to validate our three concerns: latency, isolation, and failover?
[10:05] Priya: Pilot scope suggestion: 1) Reserve a small dedicated pool for top endpoints (3-4 nodes) with warmpool prewarm, 2) Configure routing with hosted fallback for non-critical routes, 3) Enable detailed observability and run synthetic and production traffic for 2 weeks, 4) Run chaos test to simulate preemption and verify graceful fallback.
[10:28] Omar: That sounds good. For the chaos test — we need a runbook. Can Redwood provide one?
[10:34] Jordan: Yes — we'll provide a chaos/failover runbook and a test plan.
[10:40] Alex: Do you have a recommended metrics list to capture?
[10:44] Priya: p95/p99 latency by route, token cost, per-tenant throughput, cache hit rate, prewarm cold-start count, and fallback ratio. We'll include a template dashboard.
[10:58] Maya: For timelines, if we get the pricing and docs this week, we could run pilot in the week of Sept 29. Is that feasible?
[11:05] Jordan: Yes — tentative pilot kickoff week of 2025-09-29; we'll aim to have proposal by 2025-09-19.
[11:12] Omar: One more networking detail — can we avoid public internet egress for model payloads? We need VPC peering and private endpoints.
[11:20] Priya: We support private endpoints and peering. We'll coordinate with your infra to set up the network path.
[11:28] Alex: (murmur) Great. Any licensing for special HW (like A100 vs H100) selection?
[11:34] Jordan: We support a range of GPU types; H100 gives better throughput for larger models but costs more. We'll include hardware tradeoffs in the sizing doc.
[11:45] Maya: Okay last bit — quality regression detection. If a quantized fallback starts to diverge in hallucination or safety, can you auto-roll back?
[11:54] Priya: We currently have automatic rollback policies triggered by regression alerts tied to prompt-based evals. You can supply critical prompt sets to be monitored.
[12:06] Jordan: Wrap up/Recap: Jordan to send pricing + burst cost model and example contract language; Priya to share architecture diagram, SOC2 summary, onboarding steps and observability dashboard template; Lighthouse to provide qps and latency targets plus pod topology export. Plan pilot week of 2025-09-29.
[12:28] Maya: Sounds good — thanks all. We'll get the requested metrics to you by next Wednesday.
[12:35] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invite for pilot kickoff.
[12:40] Meeting ends.

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions (proper nouns, acronyms) typical of automated capture. References to "Redwood Console" and "Redwood Optimize" may appear with slight name variants (e.g., "Redwood Con sole").
